nominees.name: Isao Tanihata
nominees.affiliation: Research Center for Nuclear Physics, Osaka University, Japan, and Beihang University, China

motivation: In 1985 Isao Tanihata and collaborators used radioactive beams at Berkeley to measure interaction cross sections. They found that Li-11 has an unexpectedly large matter radius. Building on this, P. G. Hansen (deceased) and Björn Jonson explained it as a weakly bound neutron halo, with valence neutrons extending far beyond the core. Jonson then led the experimental programmes at CERN-ISOLDE and GSI that established the phenomenon. Halo nuclei, including Borromean systems in which no two-body subsystem is bound, overturned the textbook picture of nuclei as compact drops with constant density. They opened the physics of the drip lines and gave rise to new universal few-body theories and effective field theories. Today they are central benchmarks for ab initio nuclear theory and the focus of rare-isotope facilities worldwide (FRIB, RIKEN, FAIR). This discovery reshaped our understanding of how the strong force binds matter at its limits.
